passage: A familiar complaint holds that the theory of natural selection is empty at its core. Its slogan, survival of the fittest, seems to define the fittest as those who survive, so that the principle reduces to the statement that survivors survive. A claim that cannot be false, the complaint continues, explains nothing; it merely relabels what happened. The objection is old, and it has a certain surface appeal, but it depends on running together two different things: the record of which organisms in fact left offspring and the properties that made them likely to do so.

Consider two moths of the same species, one pale and one dark, resting on bark darkened by soot. The dark moth is fitter in that setting, but not because it happens to have left more offspring. It is fitter because its colouring makes it harder for birds to see, and that is a fact one can establish independently, by measuring how often birds find each kind of moth on each kind of bark. Fitness, properly understood, is a propensity: an expected rate of reproduction given an organism's traits and its surroundings. Like the fragility of a glass, it is a disposition that holds whether or not it is ever displayed. A fragile glass may survive a lifetime on a shelf, and a well-camouflaged moth may die in an unlucky accident; neither fact refutes the disposition.

Seen this way, the theory makes claims that could turn out false. It predicts that when the propensities of variants differ, and the differences are heritable, the frequencies of the variants will shift in a direction one can anticipate from an engineering or ecological analysis of the traits. Such predictions are tested constantly, and some fail, which is precisely what a tautology could never do. The distinction also explains why biologists speak of drift: in small populations the lucky can outbreed the fit, and the actual record of reproduction can depart from the expected one. If fitness simply meant survival, drift would be unintelligible, since there would be no gap between expectation and outcome for chance to fill.

The critics are not wholly wrong, however. Biologists often measure fitness by counting offspring, because propensities are hard to observe directly, and careless writing can slide from the measurement to the definition. The remedy is not to abandon the concept but to keep the evidence for a disposition distinct from the disposition itself.

passage: Discussions of the unreliable narrator tend to treat it as a game of detection. A narrator tells us one thing, the novel quietly lets us see another, and the pleasure lies in catching the gap: the jealous husband who insists he is perfectly calm, the child who reports adult quarrels without understanding them. Critics have catalogued the signals by which such narrators give themselves away, the protest that is too insistent, the detail that contradicts a claim made a page earlier, and readers have learned to watch for them. On this account the device is a kind of puzzle, and a reader who has spotted the discrepancy has finished the work the book asked of her. The narrator was wrong; the reader, standing above him, is right.

This picture is not false, but it is thin. It assumes that behind every unreliable account there stands a reliable one, which the attentive reader reconstructs and then keeps. Yet the clues by which we detect a narrator's distortions are supplied by the same narrator. We infer that the husband is jealous from what he notices, what he repeats, what he cannot stop describing; we have no other witness. The true story we assemble is therefore itself an interpretation, built from the materials of the account we have decided to distrust, and we hold it with a confidence that the novel has done nothing to guarantee.

What the best uses of the device achieve, then, is not the replacement of a bad narrator by a good reader but a change in how the reader regards narration as such. Having learned to read one voice against itself, we begin to notice how much we ordinarily grant to voices that give no sign of strain: the calm third-person narrator of a realist novel, the memoirist, the friend recounting a quarrel. None of them is lying, perhaps, but all of them select, arrange and omit. The difference is one of degree rather than kind; the narrator we call reliable is simply one whose selections we have not thought to question. The unreliable narrator makes visible a condition that reliable narration merely conceals.

It must be admitted that not every novel built on an untrustworthy teller rises to this. Some use the device as a trapdoor, a revelation held back for the final chapters that turns everything before it into misdirection. Such books can be thrilling once. On a second reading, however, they tend to go flat, because the only question they posed has been answered. The novels that survive rereading are those in which the distrust never quite settles, in which the reader, having caught the narrator out, is left wondering what she herself has failed to see.

passage: Arguments about gentrification tend to collapse into a single question: are the people who lived in a neighbourhood forced out when wealthier newcomers arrive? The question has the merit of being answerable, at least in principle. One can follow households over time, count how many leave, and compare the rate with that in neighbourhoods that have not changed. Suppose such a count found that long-standing residents of a gentrifying district left no faster than residents of similar districts elsewhere. Many would conclude that the harm of gentrification had been exaggerated, and that what remained of the complaint was mere nostalgia.

That conclusion would be premature, because it assumes that the only way to lose a neighbourhood is to leave it. Consider the resident who stays. The grocer who extended credit has been replaced by a shop whose prices assume another income; the bench outside it, once a place to sit for an afternoon, now draws the attention of a security guard; the park is the same park, but the conduct expected in it has quietly changed, and complaints to the police now come from people she does not know, about behaviour that was ordinary a decade ago. She has not moved, and no count of departures will register her, yet the place in which she lives has been withdrawn from her as surely as if she had. To call this nostalgia is to mistake a loss of standing for a loss of scenery.

The difficulty is that the language best suited to describing this loss, the language of a neighbourhood's 'character', is also the language most readily turned to the opposite purpose. Affluent districts invoke their character to resist new housing, to keep out flats that might bring poorer residents, to preserve a streetscape that functions, whatever its owners intend, as a barrier. If character means the look of the buildings and the tone of the streets, then the long-standing resident and the exclusionary homeowner are making the same argument, and it is not one that deserves much sympathy.

The way out is to locate character not in the fabric of a place but in the relations it sustains: who is able to use it, on what terms, and with what claim to be heard. On this view, what the staying resident has lost is not a familiar shopfront but the practical standing she once had in her own street, and what the exclusionary homeowner defends is not a set of relations at all but the absence of people who might form new ones. The distinction will not settle every case, and it asks more of planners than a count of departures does. But it allows us to take the quieter harms of gentrification seriously without lending our sympathy to every resident who would prefer that nothing near them ever changed.

passage: Few practices attract scorn as readily as offsetting. A traveller who pays a fee to have trees planted in compensation for the emissions of her flight is compared, almost by reflex, to the sinner who once bought a pardon: she has not stopped doing the harmful thing, the critic says, she has merely paid to feel better about it. A sharper version of the objection imagines a man who wishes to be unfaithful to his wife and pays a friend to remain faithful to his own, so that the total quantity of fidelity in the world is unchanged. If that arrangement is absurd, and it plainly is, why should paying for trees be any different?

The comparison is instructive, but not in the way the critic intends. Infidelity wrongs a particular person, and the wrong consists in what is done to her; another couple's faithfulness does nothing to repair it, because she was never interested in the global supply of fidelity. The harm of greenhouse emissions has an entirely different structure. It does not fall on anyone in particular by virtue of a relationship with the emitter; it arises from the total concentration of gases in the atmosphere, to which every tonne contributes equally regardless of where it came from. A tonne removed in one place cancels a tonne added in another as far as the eventual damage is concerned. Where a harm is aggregate and interchangeable in this way, compensation elsewhere is not a moral sleight of hand. It is, at least in principle, a genuine undoing.

What the fidelity case shows, then, is that offsetting is incoherent for directed wrongs and coherent for aggregate ones. One cannot offset an insult to a colleague by being kind to a stranger, but one can offset a contribution to a shared stock of harm by subtracting an equal amount from it. The serious questions about carbon offsetting are therefore not philosophical but practical: whether the trees would have been planted anyway, whether they will survive long enough to hold the carbon they are credited with, whether the accounts of the scheme can be trusted. An offset that fails these tests is not a pardon; it is simply a fraud, and the right response to it is an audit, not moral disdain.

I do not want to claim that nothing remains of the critic's unease. A person who comes to regard every harm as purchasable may lose the habit of asking whether she should be doing the harmful thing at all, and a culture of easy offsetting may slow the changes in conduct that will ultimately be needed. These are real worries. But they concern the character of the offsetter and the politics of reform, not the question of whether the harm itself has been undone, and they should not be dressed up as proof that offsetting is a confidence trick.

passage: Few proposals in development policy provoke as reliable a reaction as giving poor households money with no strings attached. The objection usually arrives before the argument has been heard: the money will be drunk, gambled or otherwise wasted. It is worth noticing how rarely this suspicion is applied to other recipients of public money: pensioners are not asked to show receipts, and a tax refund arrives without an accompanying lecture on how it ought to be spent. The worry is reserved for people whose poverty is taken, often without anyone saying so, as evidence that they cannot be trusted with choices.

The suspicion has been tested more often than its persistence would suggest. Evaluations of cash programmes in a range of poor countries have generally found little sign that recipients increase their spending on alcohol or tobacco, and many have found the money going to food, school costs, livestock, tools and the repair of homes. This should not be surprising, since a household living close to the margin knows its own most pressing constraint far better than an official in a distant ministry, and the constraint differs from one family to the next: a roof for one, a debt for another, a sewing machine for a third. A transfer in kind, or one tied to a particular use, has to guess, and it guesses the same thing for everyone.

None of this makes conditions pointless. Where the aim is a specific behaviour whose benefits fall partly on others, or arrive too late to weigh heavily with a hard-pressed parent, such as keeping a daughter in school or bringing an infant for vaccination, a condition can do work that cash alone may not. And in remote places where markets are thin, a sudden injection of money can push up the prices of the few goods available rather than raising what people can actually buy. These are genuine qualifications, and a careful designer of programmes will take them seriously; but they are reasons for attaching conditions in particular cases, argued on their merits, not grounds for a general presumption that the poor will misuse what they are given.

The practical upshot is a reversal of the burden of proof. The default should be cash, and anyone proposing to restrict its use should have to show what the restriction achieves and what it costs, including the cost of monitoring and the quieter cost of telling adults that they are not trusted. Paternalism is sometimes justified, and there will be programmes in which the case for it can be made convincingly; it should not, however, be the starting assumption.

passage: For most of the twentieth century, medicine described its relationship with microbes in the language of war. Bacteria invaded, the immune system defended, and antibiotics were weapons that wiped out the enemy. The metaphor was not idle decoration. It organised research around identifying a single culprit for each disease and finding a means of killing it, and that programme saved an enormous number of lives.

The study of the microbes that live in and on healthy bodies has made the war metaphor look crude. Most of these organisms are not enemies; many are useful, helping to digest food, train the immune system and occupy space that harmful species would otherwise take. An ecological vocabulary has therefore become popular: the body is a habitat, the gut is a crowded ecosystem, and health is a matter of the right community rather than the absence of germs. This vocabulary explains things the older one could not. It makes sense of why a broad course of antibiotics can be followed by a stubborn intestinal infection: by clearing out the resident species, the drug removes the competitors that had kept a harmful one in check. It also makes sense of why transferring gut bacteria from a healthy donor has proved effective against that very infection.

Yet the new metaphor carries risks of its own, and they are less often noticed because it sounds so benign. Ecology, popularly understood, suggests balance and harmony, as though every body had a single proper community to which it should be restored. Ecologists themselves are more cautious; real ecosystems have many stable states, change with season and disturbance, and do not come with a correct composition. The popular version has proved ideal for marketing. Products that promise to 'rebalance' the gut can borrow the authority of a serious science while specifying nothing that could be measured, and the vagueness of the promise protects it from ever being shown false.

The lesson is not that medicine should return to the language of war, nor that metaphors can be avoided. Every science thinks partly through images, and the choice is between images that sharpen questions and images that blur them. The ecological picture is valuable when it brings with it the working concepts of ecology, such as competition, succession and the effects of disturbance, which generate predictions that can be tested. It becomes a liability when it brings only the mood of ecology, a feeling of harmony that no experiment could ever contradict.

passage: It has become common to describe the fashion for owning less, the bare room, the small wardrobe of good clothes, the ritual of discarding whatever does not earn its place, as a revolt against consumer society. Its advocates present it as a turn from having to being; its critics, when they bother, dismiss it as one more passing style. Both responses take the movement at its word, as a stance towards consumption. Neither asks what owning little communicates, which is a different question from what it intends.

At the end of the nineteenth century the economist Thorstein Veblen described how the wealthy display their standing through conspicuous consumption, spending visibly on what serves display rather than use. The sparse interior seems at first to invert his picture. Yet emptiness has its own costs, and they are not evenly distributed. A bare floor in a crowded city is a quantity of expensive space left deliberately unfilled. A wardrobe of a dozen garments presupposes that each is durable enough, and the owner's life predictable enough, to require no more. Above all, the confident discarding of objects depends on the assurance that they can be replaced when needed. Households that live close to scarcity keep things, the spare part, the old jar, the coat a size too large, because they cannot count on being able to buy them again; for them, accumulation is a form of insurance. To throw away freely is to display that one has no need of such insurance.

It does not follow that those who embrace minimalism are hypocrites whose real aim is to impress. That objection confuses motive with function. A practice can be sincerely chosen for its own reasons, calm, order, a dislike of waste, and still operate socially as a signal that its practitioners neither chose nor want. Many who pare down their possessions are doing exactly what they say. The point is rather that the meaning of a pattern of consumption is not fixed by the consumer's intention; it is fixed by what the pattern makes legible to others, and what restraint makes legible, in a society where most people cannot afford its preconditions, is security.

The more consequential lesson concerns the hope of opting out. If even refusal can be read as a position within the system of display, then consuming less is not, by itself, an exit from that system; it is a move within it, and often one available only to those already well placed. This is not an argument for consuming more. It is an argument for suspicion towards any claim that a change in private taste can amount to a social critique, since the field of taste has repeatedly proved able to absorb its own refusals and return them as distinctions.

passage: An old explanation of fashion holds that it trickles down. Those at the top of a society adopt a new style to mark themselves off; those just below copy it, hoping to borrow some of the prestige; and once the style has spread far enough to lose its power to distinguish, the people at the top abandon it for something else. Fashion, on this account, is a chase that can never end, because the very success of imitation destroys the value of what is imitated.

The obvious objection is that much of what is worn today did not begin at the top. Jeans were work clothes; the hooded sweatshirt was athletic gear; a great many styles that now appear on expensive runways were first worn by the young, the poor or the marginal, and were adopted by designers only later. If fashion so often bubbles up rather than trickling down, the old theory seems simply mistaken about the direction in which influence travels, and with it, one might suppose, about everything that followed from that direction.

But direction was never the heart of the theory. Its real claim was that fashion is driven by a double motive, the wish to belong and the wish to stand apart, and that the two cannot both be satisfied for long. That claim survives the reversal untouched. When a luxury house borrows the clothing of a street subculture, it is not abandoning distinction but finding a new source of it: the style carries a borrowed credibility that a conventional luxury garment lacks, and wearing it signals a knowingness that cannot be acquired simply by paying more. The members of the subculture, for their part, frequently drop the style once it appears in expensive shops, for precisely the reason the old theory would predict.

What has changed is the speed. When copies of a new look can reach inexpensive shops within weeks, visible novelty becomes a weak marker of status, since it is available to almost anyone almost at once. Increasingly, those who most wish to stand apart do so not by wearing what is new but by having had it first: by access to small releases that sell out in minutes, by acquaintance with designers before they are celebrated, by knowing what is coming rather than displaying what has arrived. The chase continues; it has simply moved to ground where the pursuers find it harder to follow.

passage: Every few years a new generation is given a name, and with the name comes a character. One cohort is said to be idealistic and later complacent, another cynical, another anxious, entitled or unusually attached to its telephones. The labels are used by marketers, journalists and employers with a confidence that would be remarkable in any other classification of human beings. We would hesitate to say that everyone born under a given star sign shares a temperament; we say something not very different, and with far less hesitation, about everyone born within a given span of fifteen years. The labels are also remarkably durable: once a cohort has been named and described, the description tends to follow it into middle age, revised only when a newer cohort arrives to take its place as the subject of worry.

The trouble begins with a problem of method that social scientists have long recognised. When one group of people differs from another, the difference may reflect their age (the young almost everywhere change jobs more often than the middle-aged), the period in which they are observed (everyone, of whatever age, was affected by a recession or a new technology), or the cohort into which they were born, meaning a lasting imprint left by the conditions of their early years. Only the last is a generational effect in the strict sense. But the three are bound together by arithmetic: a person's age is simply the current year minus the year of birth, so that once any two are known the third is fixed. No set of observations can by itself pull them apart; some assumption from outside the data is always required. Much of what is confidently attributed to a generation turns out, on inspection, to be what people of that age have always done, or what people of every age were doing at the time.

A second difficulty concerns boundaries. The years at which one generation is said to end and the next to begin are chosen by convention, and different sources disagree about them by several years. A person born on the last day of one span and a person born on the first day of the next are assigned different characters, while two people born fourteen years apart within one span are assigned the same. Differences within a labelled cohort, by class, region, education and much else, are typically far larger than the differences between cohorts, which is to say that the label groups people along the axis on which they least differ.

None of this shows that generations are a fiction. There is a serious idea buried under the marketing: that people who come of age during a war, a depression or a political upheaval may carry its mark for life, and may differ in lasting ways from those who met the same events earlier or later in their lives. Such effects have been found, and they are not trivial. But they are anchored to events rather than to calendars; they mark some members of a cohort far more deeply than others, depending on where and how the event touched them; and they rarely produce a single character that an entire cohort shares.

Why, then, do the calendar labels persist? Part of the answer is that they are convenient, turning a tangle of causes into a story with protagonists. Part of it is that they flatter, inviting each cohort to see itself as distinctive and its elders or juniors as the problem. The cost of the story is easy to miss. When young adults find housing unaffordable or work insecure, attributing their situation to a generational temperament converts a question about economic arrangements into a question about character, and a question about character has no obvious policy answer.

passage: When a news organisation discovers that it has published something false, the conventional remedy is a correction: a short notice, often printed some days later and some pages away from the original, stating that the earlier report was wrong. Few people defend the correction as adequate, but the usual complaint, that corrections are too small and too late, misses the more interesting difficulty. Even a correction that is prominent and prompt may fail, and it may fail because of what a retraction asks the mind to do. The problem, in other words, is psychological before it is editorial, and editorial remedies that ignore this are likely to disappoint.

Consider a report that a fire in a warehouse was caused by paint and chemicals stored carelessly in a back room. A day later the paper announces that no such materials were present. The reader is now asked to give up the only explanation offered for the fire and to put nothing in its place. Minds do not handle this well. People tend to understand events as chains of cause and effect, and a chain with a link removed does not simply grow shorter; it breaks. An account with a missing link is uncomfortable, and when asked later why the warehouse burned, many readers reach for the explanation they were told to discard, not because they disbelieve the correction but because the correction left them with no story at all. The false claim survives because it was doing work that the retraction did not take over.

If this is right, the remedy lies less in the size of the correction than in its content. A retraction that supplies an alternative account, stating what did cause the fire, or at least what the investigators now think likely, gives the reader somewhere to go. Where no alternative is yet known, the correction can at least explain why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible, so that the discarded belief is accounted for rather than merely forbidden. There is a familiar worry that repeating a false claim, even in order to deny it, will make it more familiar and so more believable. The worry is reasonable, but it should not lead editors to issue vague notices that never say what was wrong; a denial that does not name its target cannot replace anything.

None of this makes corrections easy, and it does not excuse the haste that produces most errors in the first place. A newsroom that publishes a confident causal story before the facts are in has created a problem that no notice can fully undo, since the first explanation a reader meets enjoys an advantage that later ones must work to overcome. Readers who met the false cause first will often have repeated it to others, built further conclusions upon it, and forgotten where they heard it. The lesson for reporters is therefore double: be slower to supply a cause, and, when one has been supplied wrongly, be quicker to supply a better one.

passage: Why should anyone help a stranger they will never meet again? Kindness between relatives can be explained by shared interests, and kindness between neighbours by the expectation that favours will be returned. But much of human cooperation takes place between people who are neither kin nor repeat partners: the traveller who returns a lost wallet, the customer who corrects an undercharge. One influential answer is that such acts are paid for not by the person helped but by everyone who comes to hear of them. If people prefer to help those who have a record of helping others, then a good reputation is an asset, and an act of generosity towards a stranger is an investment in it. Biologists call this arrangement indirect reciprocity.

The idea has an obvious weakness, and its defenders have had to work hard to answer it. Reputation is only as useful as the information that carries it. In a small band where everyone watches everyone, deeds are seen and remembered; in a large society most of them go unwitnessed. Here language does decisive work. Gossip, often dismissed as idle, is the channel through which a person's conduct becomes known to people who never saw it, and a great deal of everyday conversation consists of exactly this exchange of judgements about absent third parties. Without such talk, indirect reciprocity could hardly operate beyond the scale of a village.

A subtler problem concerns the judgements themselves. Suppose I refuse to help someone who is known to cheat. Should observers count my refusal against me? If they do, anyone who withholds help from cheats will be punished for it, and cheating becomes safer. If they do not, observers must keep track not only of what people did but of whom they did it to and why. Models of indirect reciprocity suggest that cooperation is far more stable under the second, more demanding standard, which may help explain why people care so much about motives and context when they assess one another's behaviour.

It would be too much to say that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers. People sometimes behave generously in conditions of genuine anonymity, and laboratory attempts to show that subtle cues of being watched, such as pictures of eyes, make people more generous have produced mixed results. A defender of the reputational account can reply that habits formed in a world where anonymity was rare are not switched off merely because a particular situation happens to be unobserved. That reply is plausible, but it shifts the explanation from calculation to disposition, and it should be acknowledged as a shift. What survives is a narrower and more defensible claim: that the expectation of being talked about is one of the main forces that make large-scale cooperation possible, and that it works only as well as the talk is accurate.

passage: When a painting sells at auction for a sum that would fund a hospital, two responses compete for the headlines. The first treats the price as a verdict: the market, pooling the judgements of many informed buyers, has declared this one of the most important works of its kind. The second treats it as a scandal: the sum has nothing to do with art and everything to do with vanity, speculation and the search for places to park wealth. Each response captures something, but both share a mistaken premise, which is that the price is either a measure of artistic value or a measure of nothing at all.

A price measures what someone will pay to own a thing, and owning a painting is not the same as valuing it as a painting. The buyer acquires an object that is unique, that cannot be reproduced without losing the very property being purchased, and that carries a name capable of conferring distinction on whoever holds it. Each of these features has a market logic of its own. Scarcity helps explain why a minor work by a celebrated painter can outsell a masterpiece by an obscure one; the name explains why a newly accepted attribution can multiply a canvas's price overnight without a single brushstroke changing. In neither case has anyone's experience of looking at the picture altered.

This does not mean that prices float free of critical judgement. Over long periods, the artists whom critics, historians and museums take seriously tend also to be the ones whose works command high prices, and it would be perverse to call this coincidence. But the connection runs largely through reputation rather than through the works themselves: esteem builds a name, the name creates demand, and demand sets the price. The market thus registers critical judgement at second hand, much as a credit rating registers a company's prospects without being the same thing as its earnings.

The real danger lies in the return journey. Once prices are reported as verdicts, they begin to shape the judgements they supposedly reflect. Visitors crowd around the record-breaking canvas while the room beside it stands empty; institutions hesitate to show or lend works whose insurance values have become unmanageable; young artists learn which styles sell. A measure of ownership, mistaken for a measure of worth, ends by teaching people what to look at. Resisting that confusion requires nothing more radical than remembering what a price is the price of.

passage: Few words in journalism are now used with as much suspicion as objectivity. To its critics it names a pose: the pretence that reporters, alone among human beings, can step outside their own experience and describe the world from nowhere in particular. Put that way, the ideal is plainly impossible, and the critics are right to reject it. But it is worth asking whether that is the ideal anyone ever seriously defended. In at least one influential strand of its history, objectivity was proposed not as a description of the journalist but as a remedy for the journalist's limitations. Precisely because reporters could not be trusted to be neutral, the argument ran, they needed a method that would restrain what their partiality could do to the record.

The method in question resembled, in a modest way, the procedures of empirical inquiry. A claim was to be checked against more than one source; documents were to be preferred to recollection; and the reporter was to say where each piece of information came from, so that a reader or a rival could test it. On this understanding the objectivity belonged to the procedure, not to the person, much as a laboratory's results are trusted not because its scientists lack ambitions but because their work is arranged so that others can repeat it. A reporter with strong opinions could practise the method; indeed, the method existed for such reporters, since a reporter without opinions, if one could be found, would hardly need it.

What happened over the following decades was a quiet substitution. The discipline of verification, which is laborious and often invisible to the reader, was gradually overshadowed by a set of outward signs that were easier to display: a flat tone, a reluctance to draw conclusions, the habit of pairing every assertion with a counter-assertion. These signs were meant to signal fairness, but they could be produced without any verification at all. A story could quote two officials making incompatible claims, check neither, and still look objective. The appearance had detached itself from the practice it was supposed to indicate, and in some cases it obstructed that practice, since a reporter who had established that one of the officials was wrong was discouraged from saying so.

Much of the current attack on objectivity is in fact an attack on this degraded form, and to that extent it is justified. Where it goes wrong is in the alternative it sometimes proposes. If the remedy for false neutrality is for journalists to report openly from their convictions, readers are left to choose among the convictions of different reporters with no common procedure by which to test any of them. The proposal also concedes too much to the degraded form, accepting that objectivity simply is the flat tone and the paired quotation, and then discarding the whole inheritance on that basis. Candour about one's commitments is a virtue, but it is not a substitute for evidence; a frank partisan who has not checked the facts is no more reliable than a disguised one.

It should be conceded that method does not solve everything. Verification governs how a story is reported, not which stories are chosen, and the choice of what to investigate remains shaped by the interests and blind spots of those who make it. No procedure can remove that influence, and a newsroom that believes its method has made it neutral will be blind to it. Yet the concession limits the claim rather than defeating it. The case for objectivity understood as method is not that it makes journalism impartial but that it makes journalism answerable: it allows a reader who suspects a report to find out where it came from and whether it holds.

passage: Discussions of social capital commonly distinguish two kinds of tie. Bonding ties link people who are alike in some respect that matters to them, such as kinship, faith, neighbourhood or trade, and they supply loyalty and mutual help. Bridging ties link people across such lines, and they supply information, opportunities and the habit of dealing with strangers. Having drawn the distinction, many writers proceed to rank the two. Bridging is cast as the civic virtue that open societies need; bonding is regarded with suspicion, as the stuff of cliques, favouritism and inward-looking communities. The ranking is attractive partly because it flatters an ideal of openness, and partly because the dangers of tight-knit groups are so easy to picture, whereas their quieter contributions rarely make news.

The ranking is too quick. Consider a family that moves to a city where it knows no one except a handful of people from its home district. Those people find it a room, lend it money, explain which offices to visit and which employers pay on time. They are bonding ties in the purest sense, and without them the family might never acquire the stability from which wider contacts become possible. The first job outside the community, or the first friendship with a neighbour of a different background, frequently comes through someone who was met by way of the close circle. In such cases bonding is not the rival of bridging but its precondition.

It does not follow that close groups are always benign. The same density of ties that allows a community to support its members allows it to watch them, and the help it offers can come with a demand for conformity: marry within, trade within, think as we do. A young woman who wishes to train for an occupation the group disapproves of may find that the network which once sustained her family now stands in her way, and that the price of leaving it is the loss of everything it provided. Here the closeness that was a resource becomes a closure.

What separates the two cases is not the strength of the bonding ties but their permeability: whether membership of the close group is compatible with forming ties outside it, or is made conditional on refusing them. A policy that tried to weaken community networks in the name of integration would therefore risk destroying the very support that allows newcomers to reach beyond those networks in the first place. A better question to ask of any close group is not how tightly it binds but whether it lets its members go.

passage: Few management practices divide opinion as sharply as forced ranking, the system in which managers must place a fixed share of their staff in each band of a performance scale, so that some employees are always rated outstanding, most are rated adequate and a few are always rated poor, often with the expectation that the last group will leave. Its defenders make a reasonable case. Left to themselves, managers tend to rate almost everyone above average, partly out of kindness and partly to avoid difficult conversations, and a scale on which everyone scores highly conveys no information at all. A forced distribution, on this view, simply obliges managers to say what they already know.

The difficulty is that the system assumes far more than it appears to. It assumes, first, that performance within each team is spread along a curve, so that any group of a dozen people must contain its stars and its laggards. In a large population this may be roughly true, but a small team may have been assembled precisely because all its members are good, and forcing a distribution upon it manufactures distinctions that the work itself does not support. It assumes, second, that performance belongs to individuals, when in most organisations the results that matter are produced by people working together, and the contribution of any one of them is hard to separate from that of the rest.

The second assumption matters most, because of what the system teaches. If my rating depends on being ranked above my colleagues, then helping a colleague is a cost to me, and sharing an idea is a gift to a rival. The employees who learn this lesson fastest are not necessarily the most capable; they are the most attentive to how they appear. Over time, able people may also learn to avoid strong teams, since a good performer is safer among weaker colleagues than among excellent ones. A system introduced to reward merit ends by rewarding position.

It would be too strong to say that forced ranking never does any good. In an organisation where years of inflated ratings have left no way of distinguishing good work from bad, a single round of hard comparison may expose problems that polite evaluation had concealed. The harm comes when a jolt is turned into a permanent regime, and the habits of comparison it encourages become the ordinary way in which colleagues regard one another.

options.A: Employees overestimate their own performance and resent any rating below outstanding, which makes appraisals difficult to hold.
options.B: Managers, out of kindness or to avoid awkward conversations, rate nearly everyone above average, so the ratings convey nothing.
options.C: Managers rate their own friends more generously than other staff, so that ratings come to reflect loyalty rather than performance.
options.D: Teams tend to hide the weak performance of individual members by presenting all of their results as joint work.

questions.question: According to the passage, defenders of forced ranking argue that it corrects which tendency?

options.A: become more cooperative than other teams, because its members would know that each of them was equally capable.
options.B: be recognised as exceptional and therefore exempted by senior managers from the requirement to rank its members.
options.C: improve further, because competition among able colleagues for the top ratings would push each of them to work harder.
options.D: find it harder to keep and attract able people, since some of its good members must still be rated poorly.

questions.question: The passage implies that, under a permanent system of forced ranking, a team made up entirely of strong performers would most likely

options.A: Teams that shared ideas freely produced better results than teams that did not, whether or not their firms used forced ranking.
options.B: Employees who left their firms after receiving a poor rating under forced ranking usually found comparable jobs within a few months.
options.C: Where forced ranking is used, the rank of each employee depends chiefly on colleagues' accounts of how much that person helped them.
options.D: Managers in firms that use forced ranking report that appraisal meetings have become more uncomfortable than they were before.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that forced ranking discourages cooperation?

options.A: ironic, suggesting that the defenders do not really believe the argument they put forward and have other motives for it.
options.B: approving, since the author ends by agreeing that managers should be obliged to say what they already know about their staff.
options.C: fair-minded, presenting the case as reasonable before examining what it takes for granted.
options.D: dismissive, presenting the case only in order to show that it rests on a misunderstanding of what ratings are for.

passage: Translators of the great books of the past often remark on a puzzle. The original of an old epic or a classical tragedy does not seem to age; readers return to it century after century and find it as alive as ever. Yet translations of the same work date quickly. A version that seemed fresh to its first readers can sound stiff or quaint within a lifetime, and every generation or two a new one appears, prefaced by the claim that its predecessors have become unreadable. Why should the copy age when the original, which is older and in many ways stranger, does not? The question is worth more attention than it usually receives, because the answer says something about what a translation is.

The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment, with that moment's idioms and its notions of what sounds dignified and what sounds plain, and these change. The original, by contrast, has been absorbed into a tradition that reads it as a historical text and forgives its strangeness. There is truth in this, but it cannot be the whole story, since old translations are often perfectly intelligible and still feel inadequate.

A deeper reason lies in what translation requires. A great work is full of places where its sense is undecided: a word that could mean anger or grief, a line whose tone could be mocking or tender, a scene whose moral weight is left to the reader. The original can leave such places open, and much of its power to sustain rereading comes from that openness; a translator has no such freedom, because writing in another language forces choices at every point, and each choice settles a question the original left unsettled. The choices are not arbitrary, but they are shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important, and so the translation records one generation's reading of the work. When the concerns of that generation fade, its translation comes to look like what it always was: an interpretation.

Seen in this light, retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed. It is one of the ways a classic stays alive, each version making a fresh set of decisions and so showing a new reader something the others concealed. There is even an occasional reversal. Some translations become works of literature in their own right, read not as windows onto the original but for their own sake, and these, curiously, stop ageing in the way translations usually do; they come to be read, like originals, as historical texts. Their choices no longer look like a period's mistakes about another book; they look like the permanent features of a book of their own.

options.A: each generation of readers demands a translation that reflects its own concerns and preoccupations.
options.B: the originals are now read mainly by scholars, who are unusually tolerant of difficult and archaic language.
options.C: a translation uses the idiom of its own time, which changes, while the original is read with allowance for its age.
options.D: translators of earlier generations were simply less skilled, and less faithful to their originals, than the translators who are at work today.

questions.question: According to the passage, the 'usual answer' to why translations age is that

options.A: Great works can never be adequately translated, because no translator is able to preserve their openness.
options.B: The best translations are those that become works of literature in their own right and so stop ageing.
options.C: Translations date because each must settle what its original leaves open, and so preserves one period's reading of it.
options.D: Translations date chiefly because the idioms of the language into which they are made keep changing over time.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: its language, though understandable, sounds too formal and dignified to a modern reader's ear.
options.B: the decisions it made about undecided passages reflect concerns its present readers no longer share.
options.C: it was made from an unreliable copy of the original that later scholarship has corrected.
options.D: its translator misread the original language at important points and introduced errors.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an old translation which is 'perfectly intelligible' may 'still feel inadequate' because

options.A: A painting darkens as its varnish yellows with age, so that restorers must clean it every so often to recover its original colours.
options.B: A dictionary is revised every few decades to record the words and senses that have entered the language since its last edition.
options.C: Actors staging an old play must decide how each ambiguous line is spoken, so every production shows its own era's reading while the script stays open.
options.D: A historian rereads old letters and finds that a phrase she took for sarcasm was, in its own period, an ordinary courtesy.

passage: A man resolves to give up sweets, believes sincerely that he should, and then, at the end of a long and exhausting day, eats the cake anyway. The episode is so ordinary that its strangeness is easy to miss. If he really judged that refusing was better, what moved him to do otherwise? One very old answer is that nothing did: no one knowingly chooses the worse course, and the man must have ceased to believe, at least temporarily, that refusing was better. Most people find this answer too clever by half. They are convinced that they have acted against their own considered judgement, and they describe the experience in the vocabulary of force, of being overcome by something stronger than resolution.

The popular picture that develops from this description treats the will as a kind of muscle. Judgement indicates the direction, and the will either possesses the strength to follow or it does not; lapses are failures of strength, to be corrected by training, rest or improved nutrition. The picture has the merit of matching how lapses feel, and it explains why they cluster at the end of tiring days. But it makes the lapse strangely external to the person, as though desire were a weight imposed from outside and the self merely a lifter who happened to be exhausted that particular evening.

Closer examination of such moments suggests a different interpretation. The man with the cake does not usually go on thinking, clearly and vividly, that he should refuse while his hand reaches out. Instead his attention narrows: the considerations favouring refusal, which seemed compelling in the morning, become abstract and distant, while the cake is immediate, particular and present. He does not abandon his judgement so much as stop looking at it. On this interpretation the lapse is neither a mere deficiency of strength nor a simple change of mind but a failure to keep one's own reasons in view.

This does not mean that fatigue is irrelevant, or that every lapse is a matter of attention; some temptations are simply strong, and some people are considerably more depleted than others. But the attentional account has a practical advantage. If lapses were exclusively failures of strength, the only remedy would be additional strength. If they are often failures of attention, the remedy can be arrangement: keeping one's reasons concrete, placing the cake out of sight, deciding in advance what one will do when the moment arrives. People who manage their weaknesses successfully tend to do precisely this, and the muscle picture has trouble explaining why such strategies work.

options.A: show that most people lack the willpower needed to keep their resolutions about food.
options.B: establish the old view that nobody ever knowingly chooses the worse of two courses.
options.C: present an ordinary lapse whose puzzling features the rest of the passage sets out to explain.
options.D: illustrate how tiredness at the end of a day corrupts a person's judgement of what is good for him.

questions.question: The example of the man and the cake in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: treating a lapse as something internal to the person rather than as something imposed on her.
options.B: explaining why putting temptations out of sight helps people keep their resolutions.
options.C: showing that people who give in to temptation have, for the moment, changed their minds about what is best.
options.D: fitting the way lapses feel and accounting for why they are more frequent late in tiring days.

questions.question: According to the passage, the muscle picture of the will has the merit of

options.A: still holds that refusing is better but has, in the moment, stopped keeping that reason vividly before him.
options.B: lacks the strength to act on a judgement that remains clear and vivid to him as he reaches out.
options.C: will certainly give in again unless someone else removes the cake from his sight.
options.D: has temporarily concluded that eating the cake is the better course after all.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, according to the attentional account, the man who eats the cake

options.A: People who give in to temptation usually report afterwards that they felt overcome at the time by a desire that seemed stronger than they were.
options.B: People who kept tempting food out of view and planned their responses in advance lapsed as often as people who did neither.
options.C: Lapses of resolution are considerably more frequent in the evening than in the morning, especially after demanding work.
options.D: Some temptations prove strong enough to defeat even people who have planned carefully how they will respond.

passage: Ask people to estimate a quantity they do not know, after first asking whether it is higher or lower than some number, and their estimates will drift toward that number. The effect survives when participants have watched the number being produced at random, when they are told it is meaningless, and when they are paid for accuracy. It appears among amateurs and professionals alike, in guesses about the age of a building, the price of a house or a reasonable figure with which to open a negotiation. That arbitrary numbers can move consequential judgements is now one of the least disputed findings in the study of decision-making. Why they do so is more disputed, and the answer matters more than it first appears.

The older explanation treats the anchor as a starting point. People begin at the number they are given and adjust away from it toward what seems plausible, but they stop too soon, at the first value that falls within a range they can accept. On this view anchoring is a failure of effort: the mind is a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station. The remedy follows naturally. Slow people down, ask them to think harder, give them reasons to care, and they will travel further from the anchor.

A second explanation locates the problem earlier. When we are asked whether a building is older than, say, two hundred years, we do not merely note the number; we test it, and testing a hypothesis tends to mean searching for evidence that would make it true. We recall the building's worn stone and its old-fashioned windows, and these recollections, now freshly available, shape the estimate that follows. The anchor does not set a starting point so much as select the evidence. If this account is right, effort is no cure, because a more diligent search conducted in the same direction only gathers more of the same evidence.

The two accounts are not exclusive. When people produce an anchor themselves, as when they start from a figure they already know and correct it for some difference, something like insufficient adjustment seems to occur, and in those cases encouraging effort does help. But for anchors supplied by others, which are the ones that negotiators, sellers and advocates supply deliberately, the evidence favours the selective account, and with it a different remedy: not to think harder about the number one has been handed but to think deliberately against it, by asking what would make it wrong.

options.A: participants have seen for themselves that the number was produced at random.
options.B: the anchor is mentioned only after participants have already written down their estimates.
options.C: participants have been told the correct answer to the question before giving their estimate.
options.D: the quantity being estimated is one that participants deal with every day and know well.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pull of an anchor on people's estimates persists even when

options.A: convey the older account's claim that anchoring results from adjustment that stops early for want of effort.
options.B: express the author's own preferred explanation of how numbers supplied by negotiators and sellers distort judgement.
options.C: suggest that anchors work by making certain recollections more readily available than others to the person judging.
options.D: show that people resist arbitrary numbers until they are given a financial reason to care about being accurate.

questions.question: The image of 'a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station' serves to

options.A: stay close to the anchor, because the extra search would mostly turn up more evidence consistent with it.
options.B: give the same estimate but feel less confident in it, because the extra search would raise doubts about the anchor.
options.C: move further from the anchor, because the extra time would let adjustment continue beyond its usual stopping point.
options.D: disregard the anchor entirely, because longer reflection would reveal that the number was arbitrary and irrelevant.

questions.question: On the selective account described in paragraph 3, a person given an anchor and asked to deliberate longer before estimating would most likely

options.A: Before responding, ask the seller to explain in detail how the figure was reached, so that its basis becomes clear.
options.B: Treat the figure as an obviously self-interested number that cannot influence the judgement of an experienced buyer.
options.C: Before responding, set out the reasons that might make the figure a poor guide to what the item is worth.
options.D: Before responding, take time to reflect carefully on the figure offered and decide calmly how far to move away from it.

passage: Until late in the twentieth century, many biologists expected that animals as different as a fly and a mouse would be built by largely different sets of genes. Their bodies seemed to have little in common: one has a hard external skeleton, six jointed legs and compound eyes, the other an internal skeleton, four limbs and eyes with a single lens. If form reflects the genes that make it, the reasoning went, such different forms must be made by different genes. What came instead was one of the great surprises of modern biology. A small kit of genes that direct development, deciding where the head goes, where limbs sprout and which segments become which, turned out to be shared, in recognisable versions, across almost the entire animal kingdom.

The most striking demonstrations concerned eyes. Eyes had long been thought to have evolved independently many times, so different are the eyes of insects, squid and vertebrates. Yet a gene needed for eye development in mice has a counterpart in flies, and when the mouse version is switched on in the wrong tissue of a developing fly, the fly grows extra eyes, fly eyes, on its legs or wings. The gene does not carry a blueprint of an eye. It acts more like a switch that says, in effect, 'build an eye here', leaving the details of construction to the many other genes that each lineage has in its own repertoire.

It is tempting to conclude that the evolution of form is mostly a matter of rewiring old switches rather than inventing new parts, and there is much truth in that. Changes in when and where toolkit genes are turned on can alter the number of segments, the length of a limb or the pattern on a wing without any change in the proteins the genes make. Because a single toolkit gene acts in many tissues, a change to the gene itself would tend to disrupt many structures at once, whereas a change to one of its switches can alter a single structure and leave the rest alone. This helps explain why so much evolutionary change appears to lie in the regulatory regions of the genome.

Yet the shared toolkit should not be mistaken for a shared plan. That the same switch triggers eye-building in a fly and a mouse does not mean that their eyes are, in any useful sense, the same organ; the structures downstream of the switch were assembled separately, over hundreds of millions of years, from different materials. Common genes reveal a deep common ancestry of the control system, not a common design for what is controlled. The older view was wrong to assume that different forms require different genes; the newer enthusiasm risks the opposite error, of assuming that similar genes imply similar forms.

options.A: a change to the gene would alter where its protein is made but not the shape of the protein.
options.B: changes to switches arise far more often than changes to the toolkit genes that they regulate.
options.C: switches are shared by almost all animals, whereas toolkit genes differ from lineage to lineage.
options.D: a switch can alter a single structure while leaving the others in which the gene acts untouched.

questions.question: According to the passage, a change to one of a toolkit gene's switches can be less disruptive than a change to the gene itself because

options.A: a common design for the structures that the developmental genes bring into being.
options.B: a common set of genes that decide where the head, limbs and segments of a body form.
options.C: an inherited timetable fixing the order in which each organ appears during growth.
options.D: an intention that guides evolution towards a fixed and predetermined final form.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'a shared plan' most nearly means

options.A: Concluding that the eyes of insects and vertebrates were assembled separately, since their structures differ.
options.B: Concluding that a fly and a mouse share no developmental genes because their bodies look so different.
options.C: Concluding that the hearts of two distant animals must be built alike because the same gene starts heart formation in both.
options.D: Concluding that much change in animal form has come from altered switches rather than from new proteins.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an example of 'the opposite error' described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A discovery about eyes is described, its practical uses in medicine are listed, and objections to it are dismissed.
options.B: Two rival theories of animal form are set out, the evidence for each is weighed, and one is finally preferred.
options.C: A puzzle about form is posed, several proposed solutions are rejected in turn, and the question is left open.
options.D: An expectation is overturned by a discovery, whose lesson is then accepted in part and guarded against overextension.

passage: Newsrooms once knew remarkably little about their readers. An editor could see how many copies were sold, but not which articles were read, how far, or by whom; judgements about what the public wanted were made on instinct, on letters to the editor and on the preferences of the editor's own circle. Today a screen in the corner of the room can show, minute by minute, how many people are reading each story, and a headline can be tested in two versions on live audiences, the weaker one retired within the hour. Critics regard this as the moment journalism surrendered to the crowd. The charge deserves a more careful answer than either its proponents or its targets usually give.

The first thing to say is that the numbers are not lies. A click records a real decision, made by a real person, to open one article rather than another. What it records, however, is narrower than it appears. It measures the pull of a headline at the instant of choice, not the worth of what follows, and still less whether the reader was better informed for having read it. A story that disappoints everyone who opens it can outperform one that rewards every reader, provided its headline promises more. When a newsroom treats these figures as a verdict on its journalism, it is reading a measure of curiosity as if it were a measure of value. Curiosity matters, and a story that nobody opens informs nobody, but it is only one of the things a newspaper exists to serve.

The damage done by this misreading is gradual. No editor decides to abandon difficult subjects; it is only that, week after week, the stories that perform poorly on the screen are given less space, fewer reporters and less prominent positions, and the subjects they belong to slowly thin out. Each individual decision is defensible, since space is limited and something must give way, and that is precisely why the cumulative effect is so rarely noticed until it is well advanced. Coverage of committee hearings, foreign elections and the routine work of public agencies is especially vulnerable, not because readers have rejected it but because the measure in use was never designed to register its value.

It would be naive to conclude that newsrooms should switch the screens off. The instincts the screens replaced were not neutral; they reflected the tastes of a narrow group of editors, who often mistook their own interests for the public's. Some organisations now try to measure better things, such as how long readers stay, whether they return and whether they subscribe. These are improvements, though each can be gamed in its turn. The deeper lesson is that no figure, however refined, can settle what a public needs to know. Metrics can tell editors what readers choose; deciding what deserves to be offered remains a judgement that cannot be handed to the instruments.

options.A: how strongly a headline draws a reader at the moment of deciding which article to open.
options.B: the importance that editors attach to a story compared with the other stories on the page.
options.C: how many of the readers who opened a story were disappointed by what they found in it.
options.D: how much better informed a reader has become after finishing the article that the headline introduced.

questions.question: According to the passage, the click on a headline measures

options.A: editors have concluded after deliberation that such subjects are no longer worth the effort of reporting.
options.B: such stories cost far more to produce than the lighter stories that tend to perform well on screens.
options.C: resources follow a measure that cannot register the value such coverage has for readers.
options.D: readers have shown through their choices over many years that they no longer want to read it.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that coverage of foreign elections tends to shrink mainly because

options.A: Audience figures have damaged journalism, and newsrooms would serve the public better by returning to editorial instinct.
options.B: Audience figures record genuine choices but are misused when newsrooms treat them as a verdict on value.
options.C: Refined measures such as return visits and subscriptions can at last settle what a public needs to know.
options.D: Headline testing misleads readers by promising stories that the articles behind the headlines fail to deliver.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Stories about committee hearings draw fewer clicks than stories about celebrities, although their readers stay with them longer.
options.B: In newsrooms that never adopted live audience figures, coverage of the same subjects declined over the same years at the same pace.
options.C: Headline testing has raised the total number of readers that most news websites attract each month, sometimes by a wide margin.
options.D: Some editors privately regret the shrinking space given to foreign elections but feel unable to do anything to reverse the trend.
